note: An eBhāratī e-text exists locally. Wikipedia confirms that the first chapter of the (southern) Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣad is identical to the first chapter of the ancient Kaṭhaśruti, and that Olivelle counts it among the older Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads. It is one of Schrader's twenty (1912), which could be added as an edition. It is not in the 120-Upaniṣad e-text.

A local eBhāratī e-text (Ebharati-9567, Deccan College) exists, with the four seats by direction, the Daśanāmī name-endings (bhāratī, tīrtha, sarasvatī, giri …) and the great sayings. Its scholarly dating ('late; post-Śaṅkara maṭha tradition') is plausible but could not be checked.

Lubin's critical edition (The Nīlarudropaniṣad and the Paippalādasaṃhitā, with Nārāyaṇa's Dīpikā) confirms three sections, 26 stanzas, taken from the Paippalāda Saṃhitā, with Nārāyaṇa's commentary. An eBhāratī e-text exists locally.

queries: Kaula Upanishad Bhaskararaya commentary Tantrik Texts XI
note: The edition is confirmed locally: eBhāratī's copy of Tantrik Texts vol. XI (1922, ed. Sītārāma Śāstrī; introduction signed Arthur Avalon, 23 July 1922) prints the Kaulopaniṣad with Bhāskararāya's commentary, and archive.org lists the same volume.

Extant: a local eBhāratī e-text, and it is printed in Tantrik Texts XI (1922). That volume's introduction says the Kālikā gives the mantras and yantras of Kālī and prescribes Kaula sādhanā. It is outside the Muktikā. The volume could be given as an edition; the entry has none.
No. 114 of the e-text, with colophon 'ityātharvaṇīyā piṇḍopaniṣat'. The content (the departed as haṃsa; the ten piṇḍas build the new body) is located in vv. 1-2 onward.

No. 112 of the e-text (Atharvan colophon). The etymologies (gopī as protector; candana as cause of the bliss of Brahman) are located. Jacob's Atharvaṇopaniṣadaḥ (1916, with Nārāyaṇa's Dīpikā; local eBhāratī copy) also edits the Gopīcandana.

The two parts are nos. 109 and 110 of the e-text, both with Atharvan colophons. Note: the 'Oṃ, this all is the one syllable' opening is in the uttara part, not pūrva 1; see the check of tea:ganesatapani-upanisad:purva-1.

queries: Upanishad Brahmayogin Kanchipuram 18th century Ramachandrendra commentaries 108 Upanishads
note: This was on the skeleton's least-sure list; it is confirmed. The initiation name was Rāmacandrendra Sarasvatī, so the '(?)' in alt_names can be dropped; he was also called Upaniṣad-brahmendra and Upaniṣad-brahman. He was initiated by Vāsudevendra Sarasvatī at Kāñcīpuram and founded the Upaniṣad Brahmendra maṭha. He is dated to the mid-18th century, and his Muktikā commentary was completed in 1751, which fits '18th c.'. He commented on all 108 Muktikā Upaniṣads.

queries: Narayana Dipika Atharvana upanishads date Jacob
note: Existence and works are confirmed: Dīpikās on Atharvan and minor Upaniṣads, in Jacob's 1916 edition and Lubin's Nīlarudra. His dates are unknown, as the entry says; Jacob notes that next to nothing is known of him. He quotes Śaṅkarānanda (wisdomlib), so he is later than Śaṅkarānanda.

queries: Shankarananda Advaita teacher of Vidyaranya Upanishad dipika commentary
note: This was on the skeleton's least-sure list. Śaṅkarānanda, c. 13th-14th c., wrote Upaniṣad-dīpikās and the Ātmapurāṇa and was a pupil of Ānandātman. Sources call him the guru of Sāyaṇa and, in tradition, of Vidyāraṇya. The entry's 'c. 14th c.' is compatible.

Confirmed as Rāmānuja's first teacher in tradition, a Bhedābheda Vedāntin, and author of the Yatidharmasamuccaya (ed. Olivelle 1995). On the text's date (11th vs 12th c.) see the check of src:yatidharmasamuccaya.
Confirmed as the author of the Yatidharmaprakāśa (Olivelle 1976-77). The entry gives no dates.

This was on the skeleton's least-sure list. The local e-text of the Haṃsa reads 'sanatsujāta uvāca', which confirms the entry for this recension. The Adyar 1920 edition (Muktabodha M00107, with Brahmayogin's commentary) reads 'sanatkumāra uvāca', and Brahmayogin's commentary also names Sanatkumāra. The attribution to Sanatsujāta therefore holds only for the e-text recension. The entry hedges with 'in this recension', which is correct; a reviewer may wish to add the variant.

The Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads are confirmed as a recognized corpus and renunciation as a living institution (Olivelle 1992; Wikipedia). The dating fits Olivelle: the older texts are pre-300 CE and the later ones c. 12th-15th c., mostly in Advaita milieus. The distinctive positions were located in the e-text: Jābāla 4 (renounce the same day), Maitreya 2.17, Jābāla 5, Paramahaṃsa, Śāṭyāyanīya 6-11, Nāradaparivrājaka 5, Jābāla 6 and Avadhūta 2. The transmission to Daśanāmī and Śrīvaiṣṇava tridaṇḍins is the entry's own claim and is plausible; it was not checked further.

The cited passages are located: Maitreya 2.1 (deho devālayaḥ … so'haṃbhāvena), 2.14 (the sun of consciousness), 2.17; Nāradaparivrājaka 8 (the sixteen-measured praṇava), 9 (brahmasvarūpa, neti neti) and 5 (not by staff or garb). 'Avadhūta 1' is cited for 'the jīva is Śiva', but Avadhūta 1 is the etymology of 'avadhūta'. The Śiva identity is in Maitreya 2.1 and Skanda 6-10.

The e-text opens with three verses: Gautama's question (v. 1), the answer (v. 2), and v. 3 'anākhyeyam idaṃ guhyaṃ yogināṃ … bhuktimuktiphalapradam', which the paraphrase also covers. The e-text names the answerer Sanatsujāta; the Adyar 1920 edition (Muktabodha M00107) reads Sanatkumāra.

In the e-text the Haṃsa has vv. 1-3 and then two prose sections numbered 1 and 2. There is no section '3'. The pervasion passage (atha haṃsaparamahaṃsanirṇayam … yathā hy agniḥ kāṣṭheṣu tileṣu tailam iva) is in prose section 1; it is Adyar §§4-5.
The ascent (gudam avaṣṭabhya … brahmarandhraṃ dhyāyan trimātro'ham) is in e-text prose section 1; it is Adyar §6.
The mantra's seer, metre and deity and the count of 21,600 are in e-text prose section 2; they are Adyar §§10-12.
The haṃsa pictured as a bird (agnīṣomau pakṣāv oṃkāraḥ śiro bindus tu netram) is in e-text prose section 2; it is Adyar §14.
The eight-petalled heart lotus with the states is in e-text prose section 2; it is Adyar §§7-8, where it comes before the mantra.
The ten nādas (ciṇī … meghanāda; 'navamaṃ parityajya daśamam evābhyaset') are in e-text prose section 2; they are Adyar §§15-17. Neither numbering has a section '4' for them.
The effects of the ten sounds (prathame ciñciṇīgātram …) and the dissolution of mind are at the end of e-text prose section 2; they are Adyar §§18-21.
